title: Saving Private Ryan
synopsis: Omaha Beach, June 6, 1944. The ramp goes down. By the next week you're crossing France for one man whose brothers all died. Earn this.

nodes.text: Spray, vomit, prayer. The ramp goes down. Beach is already waiting. What changes is whether “Lead off” or “Go side” is the instinct you carry into it. In The Boat, the safer route is disappearing faster than the danger.

choices.consequence: You lead off. The route to Beach opens fast, while the margin for a second attempt disappears.
You choose to go side. By Beach, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

nodes.text: Water, blood, sand. The seawall ahead. You are unlikely to keep all three. Both choices lead to Seawall, but “Crawl up” arrives there with a different cost than “Stand and run.” At Seawall, everyone involved will know which risk you accepted.

choices.consequence: You commit to crawl up. It buys momentum toward Seawall and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.
You commit to stand and run. It buys momentum toward Seawall and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

nodes.text: Years later you stand at the cross. Your family behind you. To choose “Ask your wife if you've been a good man” means meeting Earn This; “Salute and walk” sends you toward Teaching instead. A third choice, “Take the third path,” keeps The Silence in play.

choices.text: Ask your wife if you've been a good man
choices.consequence: You choose to ask your wife if you've been a good man. By Earn This, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.
You commit to salute and walk. It buys momentum toward Teaching and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.
Some endings reveal themselves last. You choose to take the third path. By The Silence, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

nodes.text: You live a life worth earning. You marry kindly, work hard, raise children who do good. You never say much about the war. They know anyway. The road into Earn This began with “Ask your wife if you've been a good man” in Old Man at the Grave; here, that decision stops being a moment and becomes a life.

You teach high school history for decades. You don't bring up Normandy. The kids find it in books. They come to your desk after class. You answer carefully. The road into Teaching began with “Salute and walk” in Old Man at the Grave; here, that decision stops being a moment and becomes a life.

You don't talk about it. Your wife knows. Your children, eventually, know. Your grandchildren learn the soft version. The truth is, somehow, both. The road into The Silence began with “Take the third path” in Old Man at the Grave; here, that decision stops being a moment and becomes a life.
